title: Smartphone: safe teardown
summary: A dead phone gives a lithium pouch cell, two tiny speakers, a vibration motor, small magnets and spare parts for the same model. The battery is glued in: free it with its pull tabs, gentle heat or isopropyl alcohol and plastic tools, never by levering it with metal, because a bent or punctured cell can catch fire.

steps.text: Check it first, before you charge it. Look along every edge and feel the back with the back of your hand. If the screen or back is lifting, bulging or pushed out from inside, or the phone is hot or smells sweet, the battery is failing: stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium instead of this guide. If it looks normal, charge it on concrete or a metal tray where you can watch it, unplug it if it warms up, and switch it on: a working phone is worth far more than its parts.
steps.warn: Never charge, heat or squeeze a swollen phone.

steps.text: Set up outdoors, or on concrete, stone or a metal tray, away from anything that burns, with a bucket of dry sand and a metal tin close by. You need small screwdrivers and security bits, plastic opening picks or old plastic cards, a suction cup, a hair dryer, safety glasses, packing tape and isopropyl alcohol of 90% or stronger in a dropper or small bottle.
steps.warn: Isopropyl alcohol is flammable. No flames, smoking or sparks while it is open.

steps.text: If the phone still runs, use it until the battery is below about 25%, then switch it off fully. Pop out the SIM tray and take off any case.

Find the way in. Some older phones have a back that unclips and a battery that lifts out: if so, lift it out by hand or with a plastic tool, never metal, and go to the step that tapes and stores the battery. iPhones open from the screen side after you remove the tiny pentalobe screws on the bottom edge. Many Samsung and other Android phones open from the glued glass back, but some open from the screen side: check your model.

Warm the edge you will open with the hair dryer on a low setting until it is warm, not hot: you must be able to keep your hand on it. Press the suction cup near that edge, pull up gently and slide the tip of a plastic pick into the gap. Slide the pick along the edge to cut the adhesive, warming again as it cools. Keep only the tip of the pick inside: cables and the battery sit just below.
steps.warn: Too much heat can set the battery off. Keep the case under about 54 °C (130 °F): no flame, no heat gun. If the glass is cracked, cover it with packing tape first, and wear glasses.

steps.text: Lift the loose screen or back a little way to see where its ribbon cables run, then open it like a book on that side. Prop it up so the cables are not stretched. Now look at the battery. If it is puffed, its wrapper is wrinkled or wet, or you smell something sweet, stop: do not heat, pry or charge it, and follow safety_swollen_lithium.

Disconnect the battery before anything else. Undo the small screws and the cover over the battery connector (on a Galaxy S10e a screwed-on midframe comes off first), then lift the connector straight up with a plastic pick or a fingernail. Put a scrap of tape over the socket.
steps.warn: Metal tools near the connector can short the battery. Use plastic.

steps.text: Unplug the screen's ribbon connectors and lift the screen away. If you have another phone of the same model, keep it flat in a box as a spare.
Remove the battery. If you see pull tabs at its edges, pull each one slowly and steadily, keeping the strip flat and at a low angle, until it slides out. Hold the battery as the last strip lets go.
steps.warn: Don't press down on the battery or poke it with anything sharp while you pull.

steps.text: If a strip breaks, or there are no tabs, put 1–2 drops of isopropyl alcohol along one edge of the battery and tilt the phone so it runs underneath. Wait a few minutes. Then slide a plastic card under an edge of the battery and lift gently. If it holds, add a drop more and wait again. Or let the alcohol dry first, then warm the back of the case gently with the hair dryer, under about 54 °C (130 °F), and wait again. Dental floss sawed under the battery also cuts the glue.
steps.warn: Never lever a battery with any metal tool. If the cell starts to bend, stop, add alcohol and wait. A bent or punctured cell can catch fire.

steps.text: Lay the battery on dry sand in the tin, cover it, put the lid on loosely and tape over its connector. Keep the tin outdoors or in an empty shed, away from where people sleep. Let any alcohol dry for at least 10 minutes before you charge, solder or warm it. Check it as in the notes.
steps.warn: A cell that gets hot, hisses, swells or has bent goes outdoors into sand now and is retired. See safety_swollen_lithium.

steps.text: Take out the loudspeaker module at the bottom end and the earpiece speaker at the top. They are held by small screws, brackets or glue; unplug or unclip their contacts and lift them out.
Take out the vibration motor, usually near the bottom: a small coin-shaped motor glued in place, or a flat rectangular linear motor held by screws. Unplug or cut its flex cable and lift it out.

Collect the magnets. Phones with magnetic wireless charging have a set of small magnets in the back with the charging coil: ease them out with a plastic tool. Keep each magnet apart, with a card between, so they can't snap together.
steps.warn: Keep magnets away from pacemakers. Two small magnets swallowed by a child can pull together through the gut.

steps.text: Unclip the camera modules, and bag them with the logic board as spares for the same model. The board still holds the owner's photos and files.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The whole phone, if it works.** A GPS, camera, torch, voice recorder and library that charges from any 5 V USB source. Strip only phones that are dead or past repair.
- **Battery.** One lithium pouch pack at about 3.8 V nominal: 1,821 mAh (6.96 Wh) in an iPhone 8 (iFixit iPhone 8 teardown), 2,716 mAh at 3.81 V (10.35 Wh) in an iPhone X, which packs two cells into one battery (iFixit iPhone X teardown), and 10.78 Wh in an iPhone 12 (iFixit iPhone 12 teardown). The small board at the connector end is its protection circuit: keep it on. With a single-cell USB charge board from a power bank or vape (teardown_power_bank, teardown_vape), a phone cell runs a small LED light, a radio or a LoRa node. Solder leads to the protection board's pads, never to the cell's foil tabs. Charge to 4.2 V unless the label gives a different limit (test_lithium_cell).
- **Speakers.** Tiny magnet-and-coil speakers sealed in plastic boxes. Use them in radios, alarms and intercoms.
- **Vibration motor.** Coin-type motors run on about 3 V: a silent alarm or a tiny stirrer. Linear types, such as Apple's Taptic Engine, which iFixit describes as a linear oscillator (iFixit iPhone X teardown), need a driver circuit, so don't expect one to just run from a battery.
- **Magnets.** Speakers and motors hold tiny neodymium magnets. The iPhone 12 adds an array of 18 small magnets for its MagSafe wireless charging (iFixit iPhone 12 teardown). Use them for catches, tool holders and picking small screws out of dirt.
- **Cameras and screen.** Spares for the same model only: their flex connectors fit nothing else.

## Getting the battery out without a fire

- Run the battery below about 25% before you open the phone; iFixit advises this to cut the risk of a dangerous thermal event (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery).
- Heat softens the adhesive. iFixit heats the case behind a stuck battery until it is slightly too hot to touch comfortably, and warns that overheating can ignite the battery (iFixit iPhone 8 battery). This guide stops sooner, at warm to the hand, because OSHA names heat above about 130 °F (54 °C) as a way lithium batteries get damaged (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019). Never heat a swollen battery (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery).
- Use isopropyl alcohol of 90% or stronger: a few drops near the stuck strip, then a short wait before lifting gently (iFixit iPhone 8 battery). On a Galaxy, iFixit uses 1–2 drops along one edge and waits several minutes, because too much can damage the screen, then waits 10 minutes for it to evaporate (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery). Solvents are flammable: use them sparingly (iFixit swollen battery).
- Use only plastic tools near the cell, and never deform or puncture it (iFixit iPhone 8 battery; iFixit swollen battery). A damaged soft pouch cell can leak, catch fire or explode (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery).
- iFixit advises against reusing a battery once it has been taken out (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery). With no new cells to be had, reuse one only if it came out flat, unbent and unmarked and it passes test_lithium_cell. If it bent at all, retire it.
- Dropping, crushing and puncturing damage lithium cells. Some burning lithium cells can give off hydrofluoric acid, whose effect on skin may not be felt for hours (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019).

## Variations

- **iPhones** open from the screen side. Pentalobe screws sit on the bottom edge; inside are tri-point and Phillips screws (iFixit iPhone X teardown; iFixit iPhone 12 teardown). Heat, a suction handle and picks free the screen (iFixit iPhone 8 teardown). The battery sits on stretch-release strips, four on the iPhone 8 and iPhone 12; on the iPhone X the four tabs are stuck to the sides of its two cells, which makes them harder to pull (iFixit iPhone 8 teardown; iFixit iPhone X teardown; iFixit iPhone 12 teardown).
- **Samsung Galaxy S10e** opens from the glued glass back. A screwed-in midframe comes off before the battery connector can be reached, and the glued battery is freed with alcohol and gentle prying; the guide mentions no pull tabs (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery). Many other phones open the same way, but some open from the screen side: check yours.
- **Some older and budget phones** have a clip-off back and a battery that lifts out.
- Opening a sealed phone breaks its water seals (iFixit Galaxy S10e battery).
- Phones with wireless charging have a flat coil under the back (iFixit iPhone 8 teardown).

## What to leave

- **The glass back of an iPhone.** It is held by heavy glue; iFixit needed lots of heat and a razor blade, and bent the plate behind it (iFixit iPhone 8 teardown). Nothing behind it is worth that.
- **The logic board.** Almost nothing on it can be reused by hand. Keep it whole as a spare or for the owner's files.
- **The wireless charging coil.** Little use without its controller.
- **Any cell that bent, dented, swelled, leaked or rests below 2.0 V.** Tape its connector and store it in sand (safety_swollen_lithium). Don't put lithium batteries in household rubbish or recycling bins (EPA lithium-ion batteries).

## Testing what you got out

- **Battery.** If you can reach the protection board's output pads, measure DC volts. Above 3.0 V: good. 2.0–3.0 V: charge gently and watch it. Below 2.0 V: reject. Then follow test_lithium_cell.
- **Speaker.** Touch a 1.5 V cell across its contacts for a moment. A click means the coil is whole.
- **Coin motor.** Two AA cells (3 V) across its leads should make it buzz.
